title: Self-Esteem Stability Tracker
summary: Four fictional people share a self-esteem baseline and differ on everything else. Students deliver praise, criticism, success and rejection across three life domains and watch level, day-to-day volatility, domain contingency and recovery speed come apart — four characteristics that a single score collapses into one.
learningObjectives: Separate typical level from day-to-day volatility in self-evaluation.
Explain domain contingency: why the same event moves one person sharply and another not at all.
Distinguish recovery speed from both level and reactivity.
Explain why a single administration cannot distinguish a low level from a position on a recovery trajectory.
Describe variability as an individual difference rather than as a symptom.
privacy: No data collected, stored or transmitted; the tool asks nothing about the person using it, offers no questionnaire and produces no score for anybody.
accessibilityNotes: Native selects, checkboxes, radios and buttons; events are added through selects rather than by clicking on the chart, so there is no pointer-only interaction. The four series are distinguished by colour, by dash pattern and by a name printed at the end of each line, and the chart is hidden from assistive technology in favour of a visible table giving average, day-to-day SD, range and days to return to baseline. Delivered events are listed in text as well as marked on the plot. Changes announced through the shell's polite live region; reduced motion honoured; forced-colours rules provided; usable at 320px and at classroom-projector widths.
readmeTopic: Self-esteem dynamics: level, volatility, domain contingency and recovery as four separable characteristics
simulationNotes: Four fictional people over 42 simulated days on an arbitrary 0-100 scale with no norms and no clinical meaning. State is baseline plus a decaying event carry plus person-specific daily fluctuation; the four differ in volatility, in contingency across three neutral life domains, and in recovery rate. Randomness uses a seeded mulberry32 generator. The tool asks the user nothing about themselves, offers no questionnaire and produces no score for any person; low or variable values are framed throughout as characteristics that differ between people rather than as symptoms, and the page states explicitly that nothing shown is diagnostic, a screening instrument or a basis for interpreting anyone's wellbeing.
